source.title: Real-World Experience of Hepatitis C Treatment With Glecaprevir-Pibrentasvir During Pregnancy
source.authors: L. Madeline McCrary; Megan R. Curtis; Jeannie C. Kelly; Jessica Elrod-Gallegos; Patrick Kojima; Patricia Werner; Jennifer L. Mullersman; Tracey Habrock-Bach; Michael J. Durkin; Laura R. Marks
source.source_material_scope: Primary article only; no correction or supplementary source material supplied for this task.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study reports real-world outcomes of antenatal glecaprevir-pibrentasvir treatment in pregnant patients with hepatitis C virus infection.

The investigators retrospectively reviewed adult patients with HCV-complicated pregnancies who started GLE/PIB at 14–32 weeks’ gestation from March 2024 through August 2025 at a Midwestern tertiary care center.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV prescribed GLE/PIB during pregnancy

atoms.canonical_statement: Pregnant patients were offered an 8-week course of GLE/PIB after the first trimester through shared decision making, with postpartum deferral as an alternative.
Fourteen pregnant patients were prescribed GLE/PIB; mean age was 31 years and all were insured through Medicaid.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV prescribed GLE/PIB during pregnancy

atoms.canonical_statement: Ten of 14 patients prescribed GLE/PIB reported treatment completion, corresponding to 71%.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV prescribed GLE/PIB during pregnancy

atoms.canonical_statement: Among four patients who did not complete antenatal treatment, three discontinued within the first week and one did not start treatment and deferred therapy until postpartum.

population.label: Patients prescribed GLE/PIB who did not complete antenatal treatment

atoms.canonical_statement: None of the 14 prescribed patients had HIV, hepatitis B, cirrhosis, or multifetal gestation.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV prescribed GLE/PIB during pregnancy

atoms.canonical_statement: Among patients who initiated treatment with gestational-age data, the mean gestational age at GLE/PIB initiation was 25 weeks (range 18–31 weeks; n=13).

population.label: Patients who initiated GLE/PIB with gestational-age data

atoms.canonical_statement: All 10 patients who completed GLE/PIB had undetectable HCV RNA at or by delivery.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV who completed antenatal GLE/PIB

concept.text: HCV RNA undetectable at or by delivery

atoms.canonical_statement: Among eight completers with on-treatment HCV RNA measurements, all eight had undetectable HCV RNA.

population.label: GLE/PIB completers with on-treatment HCV RNA measurements

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 reports normal on-treatment ALT, AST, and total bilirubin levels in all 9 patients with available laboratory data.

population.label: GLE/PIB completers with on-treatment liver laboratory data as reported in Table 1

concept.text: Normal on-treatment ALT, AST, and total bilirubin

atoms.canonical_statement: The Results text states that on-treatment liver function tests were available in 8 of 10 completers and that none had AST, ALT, or total bilirubin elevations.

population.label: GLE/PIB completers with liver function tests according to Results text

concept.text: Absence of on-treatment AST, ALT, or total bilirubin elevations

atoms.canonical_statement: One patient who completed GLE/PIB experienced nausea that was managed with oral antiemetics.
No other adverse effects were reported among the remaining patients who completed GLE/PIB.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV who completed antenatal GLE/PIB

atoms.canonical_statement: SVR data were available for 9 of 10 completers, and all 9 achieved SVR4 or better.

population.label: GLE/PIB completers with available SVR follow-up

atoms.canonical_statement: All five completers with SVR12 testing achieved SVR12.

population.label: GLE/PIB completers with SVR12 testing

atoms.canonical_statement: The remaining completer had undetectable HCV RNA during treatment before delivery but did not return for post-treatment SVR testing; no known treatment failures were reported.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV who completed antenatal GLE/PIB

atoms.canonical_statement: No preterm deliveries occurred among the 10 completers, and mean gestational age at delivery was 38 weeks (range 37–39).

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV who completed antenatal GLE/PIB

atoms.canonical_statement: No new intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy was reported after GLE/PIB initiation among 9 patients with evaluable data.

population.label: GLE/PIB completers evaluable for new cholestasis of pregnancy

atoms.canonical_statement: No new gestational diabetes mellitus was reported after GLE/PIB initiation among 8 patients with evaluable data.

population.label: GLE/PIB completers evaluable for new gestational diabetes mellitus

atoms.canonical_statement: No intrapartum or postpartum hemorrhage was reported among the 10 completers.

population.label: Pregnant adults with HCV who completed antenatal GLE/PIB

atoms.canonical_statement: Among infants born to completers, there were no reported low-birth-weight infants, neonatal deaths or stillbirths, or NICU admissions.

population.label: Infants born to patients completing antenatal GLE/PIB

concept.text: Composite of reported neonatal safety events: low birth weight, neonatal death/stillbirth, or NICU admission

atoms.canonical_statement: Six exposed infants had available HCV screening and none had perinatal HCV transmission.

population.label: Exposed infants with available HCV screening

outcome.definition: Detectable HCV RNA at ≥2 months of age

atoms.canonical_statement: The retrospective design limited rigorous assessment of safety concerns and complete follow-up, including SVR12.
Only 10 patients completed treatment, limiting generalizability.
The study could not obtain pharmacokinetic data, limiting detailed assessment of efficacy and infant safety.
The optimal timing of antenatal HCV treatment remains unknown.
The authors conclude that their real-world findings support shared-decision-making use of direct-acting antivirals, including GLE/PIB, during pregnancy while prospective trial data are awaited.
The work was supported by NIH grants from NIAID and NIDA awarded to study authors.

L. M. McCrary and L. R. Marks reported funding from Gilead’s Frontlines of Communities in the United States program; the authors state that this program supports screening/linkage and does not fund activities beyond linkage to a first medical appointment.
